https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: NextDC has lodged an application with the Victorian government for fast-tracked approval to expand its controversial datacentre known as M3 in Footscray to cover 10 hectares. Photograph: Saeed Khan/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen NextDC has lodged an application with the Victorian government for fast-tracked approval to expand its controversial datacentre known as M3 in Footscray to cover 10 hectares. Photograph: Saeed Khan/AFP/Getty Images Datacentres - Australia Datacentre giant accused of using AI while lobbying for Victorian minister’s support for hyperscale factory Exclusive: Correspondence requests state MP Melissa Horne to lobby on NextDC’s behalf – but contains alleged AI-created errors Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Henry Belot Tue 15 Sep 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 11.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Victorian jobs minister has accused one of Australia’s largest datacentre companies of using artificial intelligence while requesting she lobby her colleague to approve a massive expansion of its “hyperscale AI factory”. Correspondence between Victorian cabinet minister Melissa Horne and the chief executive of ASX-listed company NextDC, Craig Scroggie, reveals increasing sensitivity to community concerns about datacentres before the state election. NextDC has lodged an application with the state government for fast-tracked approval to expand its controversial datacentre known as M3 in Footscray to cover 10 hectares , drawing 225MW of power and running 24/7. The datacentre’s size and proximity to homes in Footscray has led to growing complaints from local residents, who argue the government has been too quick to approve developments without considering long-term impacts on the community. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Some residential homes are within 15 metres of the datacentre’s boundary , which is zoned in an industrial area. Earlier this month, Scroggie took what multiple lobbying sources have described as an unusual approach by personally emailing the minister and encouraging her to back the project, which is being assessed by the planning minister. “I refer to you correspondence on 3 September requesting that I intercede on behalf of NextDC Limited in the decision of the minister for planning …” Horne wrote. Horne, who is a factional ally of the state premier, Ben Carroll, replied with a blunt opposition to the expansion. This is despite the state government’s long-term effort to attract more datacentre investment in Victoria. “I do not believe that it would be appropriate for me to lend my support to the application and nor do I wish to,” Horne wrote to Scroggie on Monday. NextDC has since employed a former adviser to the Brumby and Bracks Labor governments, Ken McAlpine, to conduct the company’s lobbying with the state government. Horne’s letter to Scroggie was published by Labor MP, Katie Hall, whose electorate includes the NextDC datacentre in Footscray. Hall is a long-term opponent of the datacentre’s expansion. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion The datacentre power spat highlights a hidden truth: we’re not building renewables fast enough to meet our needs | Alison Reeve Read more In her letter, Horne accused Scroggie of using artificial intelligence to write his letter, citing what she alleged to be basic factual errors. “I suggest that you review content produced by artificial intelligence more closely in the future,” Horne wrote on Monday. Scroggie and NextDC were contacted for comment but declined to respond to Horne’s letter and her allegations. Horne also declined to comment. Last month, Hall outlined her concerns about the impact of the NextDC datacentre and its expansion with the state’s artificial intelligence minister, Anthony Carbines. In April, Hall wrote to the planning minister who will ultimately approve whether NextDC’s expansion will be approved. She raised concerns for her constituents. “This includes the site’s location within 500 metres of over 800 homes, a kindergarten, maternal and child health services, and Stony Creek,” Hall wrote. “As a result, they are understandably concerned about the reliance on diesel generators during power outages, as well as the regular testing of these systems.” In 2025, Scroggie posted a video of the M3 site on LinkedIn and said the speed and the scale of its expansion were “stunning”. “We’re building Australia’s largest hyperscale AI factory purpose-built for the new AI era of accelerated computing,” he wrote. “This is how we build Australia’s digital future: speed, scale, sovereign, sustainable & secure.” In Victoria, large datacentres are eligible for fast-tracked planning approval. Decisions made by the planning minister cannot be appealed to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal. https://dailycaller.com/2026/09/06/ukrai.text: Francis Kapper Defense Reporter September 06, 2026 9:04 AM ET September 06, 2026 9:04 AM ET Francis Kapper Defense Reporter Font Size: Repeated attacks by the Russian military are hammering Ukrainian ports so hard that the nation has become effectively landlocked, according to military analysts. Ukrainian ports such as Odesa have long been the lifeline of the Ukrainian state; however, that time may be drawing to a close as Russian attacks on Ukrainian ports continue to escalate. The Russian attacks on Ukrainian ports include new jet-powered drones, cruise missiles and other ballistic missiles. “Ukrainian political leadership is always motivated to escalate, despite the fact that they are destined to lose any sort of tit-for-tat, because Russia can almost always hurt Ukraine more than Ukraine can hurt Russia ” Peter Slezkine, senior fellow and director of the Russia Program at the Stimson Center, told the Daily Caller News Foundation. “Ukraine needs to show some kind of dynamism, to paint a picture of victory, to generate effective photos and video clips in order to maintain the interest of its external sponsors. So it’s constantly searching for some new way to inflict pain on Russia, knowing that Russia will then inflict more pain in the same area on Ukraine.” (RELATED: Ukraine Hits Iranian Ship After Influencer Visit) The naval conflict in the Russo-Ukrainian war escalated sharply in July when Ukraine intensified strikes on Russian shipping in the Sea of Azov before expanding the campaign into the Black Sea. USF Birds played Battleship with the shadow fleet tankers today: The shadow fleet is leaving the chat. The battle for fuel supplies to Crimea in the Sea of Azov: 8 shadow-fleet tankers of the rf were hunted down and lit up by pilots of “Kairos” from the 414th Brigade “Magyar’s… pic.twitter.com/QLFHDsuVlW — 414 Magyar's Birds (@414magyarbirds) July 7, 2026 Ukraine dramatically increased drone attacks against Russian shipping around Crimea in July, striking more than 180 vessels and other maritime targets over roughly three weeks as Kyiv opened a new front in the naval conflict, Reuters reported, citing anonymous sources in the Ukrainian military. “Russia’s Black Sea fleet turned out to be susceptible to Ukrainian drones and pulled back, but in the mutual attacks on port infrastructure in the Black Sea, Russia clearly has the advantage because Russia has more ports,” Slezkine told the DCNF. “Ukraine is quite reliant on Odesa and access to the Black Sea, in order to get out grain and sustains its domestic economy. Although its economy is now mostly sustained externally.” Ukrainian-made FP-1 and FP-2 drones are the backbone of Ukraine’s naval offensive, Reuters reported. The FP drones are medium-range munitions manufactured by Fire Point , a Ukrainian weapons manufacturer. The Ukrainian 414th Separate Unmanned Systems Brigade “Magyar’s Birds,” frequently uploads videos on X showing the FP drones in action, attacking Russian shipping. ⚓️MoLoCHKa: +13 (🚢196 total) shadow fleet vessels were warned by fire over the course of 48 hours, July 21–22, that roaming the waters of the Azov and Black Seas in the interests of the aggressor state is ill-advised: 1 tanker, 10 dry cargo vessels, and 2 tugboats. 🌶️Between… pic.twitter.com/w1BDcvFJDb — 414 Magyar's Birds (@414magyarbirds) July 22, 2026 Ukraine’s drone campaign against Black Sea shipping has also affected non-Russian commercial vessels, including Turkish ships, prompting Ankara to summon Ukraine’s ambassador after two Turkish vessels were attacked near the Russian port of Tuapse, Reuters reported “Turkey’s position matters a lot to what Ukraine can do in the Black Sea. And for Ukrainian maritime exports to remain limited (or nonviable), Russia would have to keep this up, because it’s hit port infrastructure before, and then there was a grain deal or one thing or another,” Slezkine told the DCNF. “So , as long as Ukraine has Odesa, it has a potentially important port.” The reality of the Russian strikes on Ukraine’s port infrastructure is that it forces the Ukrainian military to divert manpower, interceptors and other munitions from forward operating units, weakening their frontline forces. “Ukraine will be forced to use interceptors regardless of the target,” retired Marine Col. and Senior Advisor at the Center for Strategic and International Studies Mark Cancian told the DCNF. “The challenge with attacks on ports is that Ukraine may need to spread its defenses out, thereby leaving gaps elsewhere.” Ukraine’s manpower situation has also deteriorated after more than four years of full-scale war, leaving the military struggling to replace battlefield losses and rotate exhausted troops. The Ukrainian military has turned to “press gangs,” or roving groups of armed men who grab civilians from the street to press them into military service. This is practiced widely throughout Ukraine, with dozens of videos online showing the brutality of the practice. 🇺🇦 5 fresh cases of the ongoing forced mobilization in Ukraine *In case #1, military recruiters started kicking a guy at the entrance of his own apartment… *In case #5, they attacked a guy in the underground… pic.twitter.com/u2F4z8chtZ — Lord Bebo (@MyLordBebo) June 14, 2026 “Odesa, Ukraine’s largest port, has operated on and off since the beginning of the full-scale invasion,” Luke Coffey, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute, told the DCNF. “But with Russia’s renewed focus on the city, I’m not sure how much diversion of air defense capabilities there will be from other parts of Ukraine or along the front line. Because of Odesa’s size, population and strategic importance, the Ukrainians have prioritized the air defense of the city and surrounding area for some time.” Both Coffey and Slezkine acknowledged that while Odesa provides a significant boost to the Ukrainian economy through grain exports, the European Union continuously props up the Ukrainian state regardless of its economic situation. (RELATED: Senate Wades Even Deeper Into Bloody Years-Long Proxy War In New Defense Bill) The economic damage is already becoming measurable. More than 90% of Ukraine’s agricultural exports normally move through the three deepwater ports of Greater Odesa, but intensifying Russian strikes have reduced their grain-export capacity from roughly 6 million metric tons per month to about 4 million, while four of the region’s 13 major grain terminals have suspended purchases, Reuters reported. Ukraine is already facing a critical shortage of the interceptors needed to counter Russia’s growing missile campaign, with allies delivering only about one-third as many air-defense missiles in 2026 as they supplied in 2025, Reuters reported. Kyiv continues to seek additional Patriot interceptors even after Washington agreed in July to grant Ukraine licenses to manufacture them domestically, while existing U.S. and European inventories have come under growing pressure from demand in Ukraine and the Middle East, according to Investing.com . “Ukraine’s Black Sea ports play an important role in sustaining the war effort because they provide a significant source of economic revenue,” Coffey told the DCNF. “But as I mentioned above, port operations have faced periodic disruptions since February 2022, and Ukraine, with assistance mainly from its European partners, has consistently found ways to plug budget gaps throughout the conflict.” The situation deteriorated further throughout August. Ukraine exported only about one-third of its potential agricultural volume during the month after Russian attacks effectively suspended agricultural exports through Greater Odesa, while alternative routes through the Danube, railways and the European Union lack sufficient capacity to fully replace maritime shipping, according to the Ukrainian Ministry of Agrarian Policy and Food . USF MoLoCHKa in action: three guided missiles from a Pantsir-S1 SAM/gun system fired at the Bird in one go, but the shadow fleet tub was hunted down anyway. +12 vessels from what remains of the shadow fleet were struck by USF Birds in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov during August… pic.twitter.com/EoV1RTJvNg — 414 Magyar's Birds (@414magyarbirds) August 8, 2026 Not all military analysts agree that Russia’s strikes amount to a sustained strategic bombing campaign against Ukraine’s maritime infrastructure. “Russia has primarily engaged in a very limited form of terror bombing rather than a targeted campaign against the ports, as far as I can tell,” Eugene Gholz, associate professor of political science at the University of Notre Dame, told the DCNF. “The only targeted campaign of strategic bombing that Russia seems to have attempted heretofore is against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, and that has had only limited effect. I do not know why Russia has not really tried to attack Ukraine’s ports so far.” Russian strikes on Ukrainian maritime infrastructure have nevertheless increased dramatically in recent months. Russia carried out 67 attacks on seaport infrastructure in July, along with 35 attacks on civilian vessels inside ports and another 22 against ships operating in Ukraine’s maritime corridor, according to the Ukrainian Ministry for Development of Communities and Territories . The attacks continued into August, with Russian forces striking seaport infrastructure five times during the first three days of the month alone, according to the ministry. The loss of access to Ukraine’s deepwater ports has consequently pushed increasing amounts of cargo toward the country’s smaller Danube ports at Reni and Izmail. Roughly 80 vessels were waiting to reach the Ukrainian ports through Romania’s Sulina Canal by Aug. 31, while Ukrainian Railways estimated it could move roughly 500,000 metric tons of grain to the Danube ports each month, Reuters reported. Those alternatives have struggled to absorb the displaced trade. Ukraine exported just 539,000 metric tons of grain between Aug. 1 and Aug. 21, compared with 1.73 million tons during the same period in 2025, while congestion and delays were costing some vessels as much as $8,000 per day, Reuters reported. Russia has also increasingly targeted the infrastructure Ukraine relies upon to circumvent disruptions at its principal Black Sea ports. Russian forces struck export facilities in the Odesa region and the Orlivka border crossing with Romania on Sept. 1, temporarily suspending the processing of vehicles and travelers at the crossing, Reuters reported. The widening attacks leave Kyiv defending not only the ports themselves, but also the railways, Danube facilities, border crossings and other infrastructure needed to keep Ukrainian exports moving when Greater Odesa is unavailable. Russia’s end goal may be to completely annex the Ukrainian coastline, Slezkine said. “Russia’s dream, of course, in this war is to deprive Ukraine of its Black Sea coast permanently,” Slezkine told the DCNF. “So I think for a lot of Russian strategists, Odessa is much more important than Kyiv. If they could take Odessa and connect with Transnistria, then Ukraine becomes a slightly larger Latvia, and then who cares? Because it’s a totally non-viable economy or military threat. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/09/latv.text: On 5 October, a group used makeshift stairs to enter Latvia. While the Baltic country of two million has faced irregular migration from Belarus since 2021, the latest incident was particularly aggressive.The group of 20 migrants was led by “armed, masked escorts openly threatening Latvian soldiers,” Latvia’s Interior Minister, Jānis Dombrava, told Euronews. In the following hours, border surveillance equipment was damaged, reducing Latvia’s “ability to detect and respond to further incursions.”“The combination of armed intimidation and targeted sabotage raises the risk of a violent confrontation and tests both our defences and our willingness to respond,” Dombrava said, adding that it’s “a security threat, not simply a migration-management problem.”Latvia completed the fencing of its 173-kilometre border with Belarus this year and installed advanced surveillance systems, making crossings harder. The obstacles are making facilitators increasingly aggressive, according to Guntis Pujāts, head of Latvia’s State Border Guard.“That’s why they are trying to be more aggressive and so to throw stones as well, to show what looks like a weapon and so on,” Pujāts told Euronews, adding that the incident “shows that the situation is not going to decrease but in the opposite way”.More powers to Border GuardThe State Border Guard is now seeking greater powers to protect its personnel and secure the country’s border, as Latvia enters its fifth year of dealing with irregular migration from Belarus. The interior minister supports the move.Currently, border guards already have the right to use firearms in circumstances prescribed by law, including when responding to serious threats and attempted acts of sabotage. Pujāts wants to broaden their powers, as well as those of police and military personnel supporting border operations, to enable them to “protect the security of Latvia”.On Thursday, the Border Guard submitted a proposal to the Interior Ministry seeking changes to the rules.Under the proposed changes, border guards would no longer have to issue a warning before using force in certain circumstances, Pujāts said. They would also be able to use the tools at their disposal to stop and “neutralise” people damaging border infrastructure.“We will not be obliged to warn before, and we will be allowed all tools that we have to stop and so to neutralise persons who are damaging our border infrastructure,” he said.The interior minister confirmed to Euronews that he will propose amendments “to give those protecting our country clearer powers and greater discretion when facing threats of this kind.”“Those who protect Latvia's state border – border guards, soldiers and other officials – must be confident that they will not be unjustifiably subjected to criminal prosecution for the lawful use of firearms or special means,” he said. Pujāts said he did not know how long it would take for the proposal to become law. Asked when he would like the changes to take effect, he replied: “Yesterday, or the day before yesterday.”
